```{python}
#| label: setup
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

import random

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import FancyBboxPatch

GRAY = "#b0b0b0"
RED = "firebrick"
BLUE = "steelblue"
SCHOOL_SIZE = 763
OUTBREAK_DATES = [
    "Jan 22", "Jan 23", "Jan 24", "Jan 25", "Jan 26", "Jan 27", "Jan 28",
    "Jan 29", "Jan 30", "Jan 31", "Feb 1", "Feb 2", "Feb 3", "Feb 4",
]
IN_BED = [3, 8, 26, 76, 225, 298, 258, 233, 189, 128, 68, 29, 14, 4]


def simulate_sir(population_size, initial_infected, beta, gamma, rng):
    """Gillespie simulation of the SIR model, until no one is infected."""
    s, i, clock = population_size - initial_infected, initial_infected, 0.0
    times, s_counts, i_counts = [0.0], [s], [i]
    while i > 0:
        infection_rate = beta * s * i / population_size
        total_rate = infection_rate + gamma * i
        clock += rng.expovariate(total_rate)
        if rng.random() < infection_rate / total_rate:
            s, i = s - 1, i + 1
        else:
            i -= 1
        times.append(clock)
        s_counts.append(s)
        i_counts.append(i)
    return times, s_counts, i_counts


def simulate_sir_euler(population_size, initial_infected, beta, gamma,
                       max_time, time_step):
    """Euler's method for the SIR model."""
    s, i, r = population_size - initial_infected, initial_infected, 0.0
    times, s_counts, i_counts, r_counts = [0.0], [s], [i], [r]
    for step in range(round(max_time / time_step)):
        new_infections = beta * s * i * time_step / population_size
        recoveries = gamma * i * time_step
        s, i, r = s - new_infections, i + new_infections - recoveries, r + recoveries
        times.append((step + 1) * time_step)
        s_counts.append(s)
        i_counts.append(i)
        r_counts.append(r)
    return times, s_counts, i_counts, r_counts


def tidy(axes, fontsize = 16):
    axes.tick_params(labelsize = fontsize * 0.8)
    for side in ["right", "top"]:
        axes.spines[side].set_visible(False)
```

## Last time

Lineages **split** (birth) and **die** (death) at random

. . .

::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
Today: The same model, but the "lineages" are **infections**
:::

. . .

-   An infected person passes the virus on: "birth" of an infection
-   An infected person recovers: "death" of an infection

::: {.notes}
0:00-1:00

Last time, the recap of the birth-death lab ended with this idea. Today we
take it seriously: an outbreak is a birth-death process, with one twist. This
deck introduces the concepts for Capstone 3, which students work on outside of
class.
:::

# The SIR model {background-color="#1b3a5c"}

## Three groups of people^[@Kermack1927]

```{python}
#| label: compartments
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 2.6
#| fig-align: center

_figure, _axes = plt.subplots(figsize = (11, 2.6))
_boxes = [("S", "Susceptible", BLUE, 0.0), ("I", "Infected", RED, 5.0),
          ("R", "Recovered", "dimgray", 10.0)]
for _letter, _name, _color, _x in _boxes:
    _axes.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((_x, 0.0), 2.2, 1.6,
                                   boxstyle = "round,pad=0.08",
                                   facecolor = _color, edgecolor = "none"))
    _axes.text(_x + 1.1, 0.95, _letter, ha = "center", va = "center",
               fontsize = 30, color = "white", fontweight = "bold")
    _axes.text(_x + 1.1, 0.35, _name, ha = "center", va = "center",
               fontsize = 15, color = "white")
for _x0, _label in [(2.5, "infection\n" + r"$\beta I S / N$"),
                    (7.5, "recovery\n" + r"$\gamma I$")]:
    _axes.annotate("", xy = (_x0 + 2.2, 0.6), xytext = (_x0, 0.6),
                   arrowprops = dict(arrowstyle = "-|>", lw = 2.5,
                                     color = "black", mutation_scale = 25))
    _axes.text(_x0 + 1.1, 0.8, _label, ha = "center", va = "bottom",
               fontsize = 16, linespacing = 1.4)
_axes.set_xlim(-0.3, 12.5)
_axes.set_ylim(-0.3, 1.9)
_axes.axis("off")
plt.show()
```

::: {.incremental style="font-size: 80%;"}
-   $N$ people: $S + I + R = N$
-   Each infected person recovers at rate $\gamma$ (on average, after
    $1 / \gamma$ days)
-   Each infected person passes on the virus at rate $\beta$, but only
    a fraction, $S / N$, of the people they meet are susceptible
    -   So, transmission rate is $\beta \frac{S}{N}$ per infected person
:::

::: {.notes}
1:00-3:00

Recovered people are immune (or isolated); either way they're out of the game.
Recovery is exactly like extinction in a birth-death model: total rate gamma
times I. Infection is like birth, with a twist: the rate per infected person is
beta times S/N, so it slows down as the virus runs out of susceptible people.
:::

## Compared to a birth-death model

::: {style="font-size: 85%;"}
| | Birth-death | SIR |
|:--|:-:|:-:|
| What multiplies? | Lineages, $n$ | Infections, $I$ |
| Total rate of "births" | $\lambda n$ | $\beta \frac{S}{N} \cdot I$ |
| Total rate of "deaths" | $\mu n$ | $\gamma I$ |
:::

. . .

At the start of an outbreak, $S / N \approx 1$, so it ***is*** a birth-death
process with $\lambda = \beta$ and $\mu = \gamma$

. . .

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
The difference: Each infection "uses up" a susceptible person, so the outbreak
slows down as $S$ shrinks
:::

::: {.notes}
3:00-4:00

Keep this table in mind; it's the key to Part 2 of the capstone.
:::

## The basic reproduction number

$R_0$: The average number of people one infected person infects, when everyone
else is susceptible

. . .

Infects at rate $\beta$, for an average of $1 / \gamma$ days:

$$
R_0 = \frac{\beta}{\gamma}
$$

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
## Question
What do you think happens when $R_0 < 1$? When $R_0 > 1$?
:::

::: {.notes}
4:00-5:00

The R in R0 is not the R in SIR. Take a couple of answers: if each infected
person infects fewer than one other on average, each "generation" is smaller
than the last. Students explore the threshold with sliders in Challenge 6.
:::

# Simulating an outbreak one event at a time {background-color="#1b3a5c"}

## The Gillespie algorithm, again^[@Gillespie1977]

::: {.incremental style="font-size: 88%;"}
1.  Calculate the total (population) rates: infection $\beta I S / N$ and
    recovery $\gamma I$
2.  Draw an exponential **waiting time** using the **total rate**
3.  Choose **which event** happened, with probability proportional to its rate
    -   Infection: $S - 1$, $I + 1$
    -   Recovery: $I - 1$
4.  Repeat until $I = 0$
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Same recipe as `simulate_birth_death`, with different rates
:::

::: {.notes}
5:00-6:00

Students write simulate_sir in Challenge 1 by adapting simulate_birth_death,
which is given at the top of the capstone. No max_time: every outbreak ends,
because each person can be infected only once.
:::

## Minor and major outbreaks

```{python}
#| label: stochastic
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-align: center

_rng = random.Random(1927)
_figure, (_left, _right) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize = (11, 4))
_maj_spread_label = "Major outbreak"
_min_spread_label = "Minor outbreak"
_n_sims = 20
_n_maj_spread = 0
for _ in range(20):
    _t, _s, _i = simulate_sir(SCHOOL_SIZE, 1, 1.0, 0.5, _rng)
    _left.step(_t, _i, where = "post", color = RED, alpha = 0.6, lw = 1.2)
    if SCHOOL_SIZE - _s[-1] < 0.1 * SCHOOL_SIZE:
        _left.step(_t, _i, where = "post", color = "blue", alpha = 0.6, lw = 1.9,
                   label = _min_spread_label)
    else:
        _left.step(_t, _i, where = "post", color = RED, alpha = 0.6, lw = 1.2,
                   label = _maj_spread_label)
        _n_maj_spread += 1
_left.set_xlabel("Days", fontsize = 16)
_left.set_ylabel("Infected", fontsize = 16)
_left.set_title("20 outbreaks", fontsize = 16)
_legend_handles, _legend_labels = _left.get_legend_handles_labels()
_uniq_legend_entries = dict(zip(_legend_labels, _legend_handles))
_annot_legend_entries = {}
for _label, _handle in _uniq_legend_entries.items():
    if _label == _min_spread_label:
        _annot_legend_entries[f"{_label} ({_n_sims - _n_maj_spread})"] = _handle
    else:
        _annot_legend_entries[f"{_label} ({_n_maj_spread})"] = _handle
_left.legend(_annot_legend_entries.values(), _annot_legend_entries.keys())
_sizes = []
for _ in range(1000):
    _t, _s, _i = simulate_sir(SCHOOL_SIZE, 1, 1.0, 0.5, _rng)
    _sizes.append(SCHOOL_SIZE - _s[-1])
_right.hist(_sizes, bins = 50, color = GRAY)
_right.set_xlabel("Total number infected", fontsize = 16)
_right.set_ylabel("Outbreaks", fontsize = 16)
_right.set_title("1,000 outbreaks", fontsize = 16)
for _ax in (_left, _right):
    tidy(_ax)
_figure.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {style="font-size: 85%;"}
$N = 763$, one infected person, $\beta = 1$, $\gamma = 0.5$ per day
($R_0 = 2$)
:::

::: {.notes}
6:00-7:30

Almost no outbreaks in between: either the virus disappears after a handful of
infections, or most of the school gets infected. Ask: what does this remind you
of from last time? (Clades that either go extinct early or grow big.)
:::

## How often does an outbreak fizzle out?

```{python}
#| label: fizzle-table
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| output: asis

_rng = random.Random(1978)
_rows = []
for _r0 in [1.5, 2.0, 3.0]:
    _minor = 0
    for _ in range(1000):
        _t, _s, _i = simulate_sir(SCHOOL_SIZE, 1, _r0 * 0.5, 0.5, _rng)
        if SCHOOL_SIZE - _s[-1] < 0.1 * SCHOOL_SIZE:
            _minor += 1
    _rows.append(f"| {_r0} | {_minor / 1000:.2f} |")
print(
    "::: {style=\"font-size: 85%;\"}\n"
    + "| $R_0$ | Fraction of minor outbreaks (simulated) |\n"
    + "|:-:|:-:|\n"
    + "\n".join(_rows)
    + "\n:::"
)
```

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
## Question
Last time, a clade starting with one lineage eventually died out with
probability $\mu / \lambda$.^[@Kendall1948]
What should the probability be here?
:::

::: {.notes}
7:30-9:00

Don't give it away completely; this is Challenge 3. (Answer: early on it's a
birth-death process with lambda = beta and mu = gamma, so mu/lambda =
gamma/beta = 1/R0: 0.67, 0.50, 0.33.) Point out the public-health meaning: one
infected traveler doesn't guarantee an epidemic, but repeated introductions
eventually get "lucky."
:::

# The average outbreak {background-color="#1b3a5c"}

## Euler's method {.smaller}

In a short time $\Delta t$, the **expected** numbers of events are:

$$
\text{new infections} = \frac{\beta I S}{N} \Delta t
\qquad
\text{recoveries} = \gamma I \Delta t
$$

. . .

Update, and repeat, one time step at a time:

$$
\begin{aligned}
S &\leftarrow S - \text{new infections} \\
I &\leftarrow I + \text{new infections} - \text{recoveries} \\
R &\leftarrow R + \text{recoveries}
\end{aligned}
$$

. . .

-   Solves the SIR ***differential equations***, *e.g.*,
    $\frac{dI}{dt} = \frac{\beta I S}{N} - \gamma I$
-   Smaller $\Delta t$ &rarr; closer to the exact solution (but more steps)

::: {.notes}
9:00-10:30

S, I, and R are now averages, so they can be fractions of people. Emphasize:
calculate both amounts before updating anything. Students write
simulate_sir_euler (Challenge 4) and their own plotting function (Challenge 5).
In Challenge 6 they try big time steps to see what goes wrong.
:::

## Random outbreaks vs. the average

```{python}
#| label: stochastic-vs-euler
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-align: center

_rng = random.Random(3)
_figure, _axes = plt.subplots(figsize = (10, 3.5))
_shown = 0
while _shown < 15:
    _t, _s, _i = simulate_sir(SCHOOL_SIZE, 1, 1.0, 0.5, _rng)
    if SCHOOL_SIZE - _s[-1] < 0.1 * SCHOOL_SIZE:
        continue
    _axes.step(_t, _i, where = "post", color = GRAY, lw = 1)
    _shown += 1
_t, _s, _i, _r = simulate_sir_euler(SCHOOL_SIZE, 1, 1.0, 0.5, 40.0, 0.01)
_axes.plot(_t, _i, color = RED, lw = 3.5, label = "Euler's method")
_axes.plot([], [], color = GRAY, lw = 1, label = "15 major outbreaks (Gillespie)")
_axes.set_xlabel("Days", fontsize = 16)
_axes.set_ylabel("Infected", fontsize = 16)
_axes.legend(fontsize = 14, frameon = False)
tidy(_axes)
_figure.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {style="font-size: 85%;"}
-   Major outbreaks have the same **shape**
    -   Randomness early on mostly shifts **when** they take off
:::

::: {.notes}
10:30-11:30

Same parameters as before (R0 = 2). Only major outbreaks shown. The early,
random phase is like the start of the birth-death simulations (most variable
near the start); once hundreds of people are involved, the randomness averages
out.
:::

## Why does an outbreak peak?

```{python}
#| label: peak
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 2.9
#| fig-align: center

_t, _s, _i, _r = simulate_sir_euler(SCHOOL_SIZE, 1, 1.0, 0.5, 40.0, 0.01)
_peak = _i.index(max(_i))
_figure, _axes = plt.subplots(figsize = (10, 2.9))
_axes.plot(_t, [_v / SCHOOL_SIZE for _v in _s], color = BLUE, lw = 3,
           label = "$S / N$")
_axes.plot(_t, [_v / SCHOOL_SIZE for _v in _i], color = RED, lw = 3,
           label = "$I / N$")
_axes.axvline(_t[_peak], color = "black", ls = "--", lw = 1.5)
_axes.text(_t[_peak] + 0.5, 0.9, "Peak of $I$", fontsize = 14)
_axes.set_xlabel("Days", fontsize = 16)
_axes.set_ylabel("Fraction of people", fontsize = 16)
_axes.legend(fontsize = 14, frameon = False, loc = "center right")
tidy(_axes)
_figure.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {style="font-size: 85%;"}
Each infected person infects at rate $\beta S / N$ and recovers at rate
$\gamma$
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
## Question
What is $S / N$ when $I$ stops growing? (You'll find out in the capstone!)
:::

::: {.notes}
11:30-12:30

R0 = 2 here. The outbreak turns around long before it runs out of susceptible
people. Don't give the answer (S/N = 1/R0 at the peak) away; it's Challenge 6,
and it sets up the herd immunity extra credit (1 - 1/R0).
:::

# The boarding school {background-color="#1b3a5c"}

## Influenza at a boarding school, 1978^[@Anonymous1978bmj]

```{python}
#| label: school-data
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| fig-align: center

_figure, _axes = plt.subplots(figsize = (10, 2.8))
_axes.bar(range(1, 15), IN_BED, color = BLUE)
_axes.set_xticks(range(1, 15), OUTBREAK_DATES, rotation = 45)
_axes.set_ylabel("Students in bed", fontsize = 16)
tidy(_axes, fontsize = 15)
_figure.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {style="font-size: 78%;"}
-   A strain of H1N1 that hadn't circulated since the 1950s: no one was immune
-   512 of the school's 763 students were confined to bed within two weeks
:::

::: {.notes}
12:30-13:30

From an anonymous report in the BMJ; the counts were only published as a
figure, so these numbers are digitized (via De Vries et al. 2006, as used in
the R package outbreaks) and vary slightly among sources. It's one of the
most-used datasets in epidemiology courses.
:::

## Fitting the model to the data {.smaller}

For each $\beta$ and $\gamma$, how far are the predictions from the counts?

$$
\text{sum of squares} = \sum_{\text{days}} \left(\text{observed} -
\text{predicted}\right)^2
$$

::: {.incremental}
-   ***Least squares***: The best fit has the **smallest** sum of squares (like
    `linregress` in Capstone 2)
-   ***Grid search***: Try every combination of $\beta$ and $\gamma$ from two
    lists, and keep the best
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
## Watch for
How contagious was this virus? And why did only 512 students end up in bed?
:::

::: {.notes}
13:30-14:30

The predictions come from Euler's method (a helper function in the capstone).
We treat students in bed as the infected group, and start with one infected student on
January 21. Students should think about whether those assumptions are
reasonable (Challenge 8).
:::

## Summary

::: {style="font-size: 90%;"}
-   The **SIR model**: infections at rate $\beta I S / N$, recoveries at rate
    $\gamma I$
-   $R_0 = \beta / \gamma$: the average number of people one case infects
-   Near its start, an outbreak is a **birth-death process**, so many
    outbreaks **fizzle out** by chance
-   **Euler's method** calculates the average course of an outbreak, one small
    time step at a time
-   Fitting the model to data tells us how contagious a virus is
:::

::: {.notes}
14:30-15:00
:::
